2.72.m: Pippala said: / Having heard Mātali's words, what did that king, / the son of Nahuṣa, do, O very wise one? Tell me that in detail.
This holy story is full of all merit and destroys sin; / I desire to hear it, O wise one; I am never satiated.
Sukarma said: / Yayāti, the best of monarchs and foremost of all upholders of dharma, / spoke to that arrived messenger, Mātali, Indra's charioteer.
Yayāti said: / I will certainly not abandon the body, nor shall I go to heaven / without this earthly body, O messenger; of this there is no doubt.
Although great faults of the body are proclaimed in this way, / and previously all good and bad qualities were related by you,
I will not abandon the body, nor will I go to heaven. / Having gone from here, say this to Purandara, the god of gods:
Indeed, neither by a solitary soul nor by a body alone, O highly intelligent one, / does worldly success in this world ever come to pass.
The body does not exist without the vital breath, nor does the soul exist without the body; / I shall not bring about the destruction of the friendship of both, O Indra.
By the gracious presence of the body alone does this vital breath enjoy pure happiness / and other pleasures pleasing to the mind.
Knowing this, O divine messenger, the enjoyment of heaven is not to be enjoyed; / highly wicked diseases causing misery arise [there].
O Mātali, old age arises from sin and from blemish. / Look at my body, endowed with merit, [as if] sixteen years old!
From my birth, my body has reached fifty years; / even so, a fresh nature of the body also appears.
My time has passed, O messenger, countless years beyond compare; / just as the body of a sixteen-year-old man shines,
so my body shines, endowed with strength and vigor. / There is neither languor for me nor decline, no weariness, diseases, or old age.
O Mātali, my body even grows through zeal for dharma. / The divine medicine consisting entirely of nectar is the supreme medicine,
which was indeed formulated in ancient times called "dharma" to destroy the disease of sin. / By that, my body is purified, and its faults are gone.
Meditation upon Hṛṣīkeśa and the excellent utterance of His name: / this elixir, O messenger, I always take thus.
Through that, my diseases, blemishes, sins, and so forth have gone to destruction. / Indeed, while there exists in the world the great medicine named Kṛṣṇa,
men, afflicted by the disease of sin, go to death; / great fools do not drink the elixir of Kṛṣṇa's name.
Through that meditation, through knowledge, through the disposition of worship, O Mātali, / through truth, and through the merit of gift-giving, my body is free from disease.
Diseases and afflictions arise for the embodied from the increase of sin. / From afflictions death arises for living beings—there is no doubt about this.
Therefore dharma must be practiced by men who resort to merit and truth. / The body consists of the five elements, worn out at its veins and joints.
In this way, a mortal is joined together like [metal joined] by a goldsmith with borax; / there shines the great fire, ever roaming as the bodily humor.
He who joins it together in its hundred fragments, O brāhmaṇa, he is wise, / by the divine name of Hari and by good fortune, O Pippala.
For those fragments made of the five [elements], worn out in their hundred joints, / are all held together by that; the body becomes balanced in its elements.
By the ritual service of Hari, by meditation, and by observance, / by truthful intention, and by giving, the body becomes fresh.
The faults of the body perish, and its diseases; listen, O Mātali! / For external and internal purity [results]; foul odor does not at all arise.
Then one becomes pure, O charioteer, through the grace of that Holder of the Discus. / I will not go to heaven; I will make heaven right here.
Through austerity, devotion, and my own duty, / I will turn the surface of the earth into heaven by the grace of that Holder of the Discus.
Knowing this, go and speak to Puraṃdara." / Sukarma said: Having heard what was spoken by the king, then the charioteer,
after congratulating the king with blessings and bidding him farewell, departed; / and he reported everything to the great-souled Indra.
Hearing [the words] of the great-souled Yayāti, the thousand-eyed [Indra] / then reflected on how to bring him to heaven.

2.73.m: Pippala said: / When that noble messenger of Indra had departed, / what then did the righteous Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, do?
Sukarma said: / When that messenger of the supreme god had departed, that prince reflected; / summoning his foremost messengers, he swiftly ordered words connected with dharma and righteousness:
"Let the foremost messengers go to the best cities, to the countries, the continents, and the entire world: / 'Let them carry out my righteous word; let the worlds go on the good path of Hari!
With holy dispositions resembling nectar, through meditations, knowledge, worship, austerities, / sacrifices, and gifts, abandoning sense-objects, let the worlds worship the one Madhusūdana!

Everywhere let them see the single Enemy of the Asuras—in the dry, in the moist, and in the immobile, / in clouds, on earth, among the moving and unmoving, and even in their own bodies in the form of the soul!
Having intended that God, let them give gifts with hospitality and ancestral rites; / sacrifice to Nārāyaṇa, the best of the gods! You will soon be freed from faults.'
Whatever man here does not cause my word to be obeyed, out of greed or delusion, / that pitiless one will surely meet punishment, like a vile thief toward me."
Having heard the words of the king, the messengers, joyful in mind, across the whole earth / proclaimed thus among the subjects the entire import of the order instituted by the king:
"Mortal men, beginning with brāhmaṇas: the holy nectar brought thus to earth by that king, / the holy [drink] named Vaiṣṇava, free from faults, with an agreeable outcome—drink it!

The glorious Keśava, dispeller of distress, the foremost, having the form of bliss, the supreme truth— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!

Him who holds a sword in hand, named Madhusūdana, the abode of Śrī, endowed with qualities, lord of the gods— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!
The glorious Lord of the Lotus, lotus-eyed, the support of the worlds, the great lord— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!
Dispelling sin, destroying disease, giving bliss, slayer of the Dānavas and Daityas— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!

The embodiment of sacrifice, holding a discus in His hand, a mine of merit, happiness, infinite in form— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!
The abode of the universe, spotless, cessation, named Rāma, delighting, enemy of Mura— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!

Sun-formed, destruction of darkness, destroyer of bondage, for the lotuses of the intellect— / the nectar of His name, dispeller of faults, has been brought by the good king; let the worlds drink it!"
That man devoted to Viṣṇu, who, self-controlled at dawn, recites this true and holy nectar of names, / that great soul goes to liberation; there is no question about it.

2.74.m: Sukarma said: / Then the messengers proclaimed in all villages, continents, countries, and cities: / "O people, hear the king's command! Worship Hari with all your might!
With gifts, with many sacrifices, with austerities, with righteous desires, with worships and minds, / let the worlds meditate upon Madhusūdana! Such is the order of that king!"
Having heard that entirely holy [order] thus well proclaimed upon the surface of the earth by the people, / from that time onward mortals worship Viṣṇu, meditate, sing, and chant [His name].
With excellent hymn-mantras composed in the Vedas and holy hymns resembling nectar, / with minds fixed on Him, they worship the glorious Keśava through vows, fasts, observances, and gifts.
Abandoning faults arising from their own bodies, minds, and speeches, all devoted to love, / they fully worship the glorious Vāsudeva, the abode of Lakṣmī, the abode of all worlds.
Thus the command of that king prevailed over the circle of the earth; / through their Vaiṣṇava disposition, all those people were victorious.
Skilled in knowledge, they worshiped Viṣṇu through names and rituals; / devoted to his meditation, determined on him, dedicated to Viṣṇu’s worship.
As far as the entire circle of the earth extends, as far as the sun shines, / for that whole extent human beings shone forth as devotees of the Blessed One.
By the power of meditating on Viṣṇu, through worship, hymns of praise, and [reciting] his name, / human beings at that time were freed from mental and physical diseases.
They were devoid of sorrow, meritorious, and rich in penance; / they all became Vaiṣṇavas, O Brahmin, by the grace of the wielder of the discus.
Free from illness, and devoid of faults and anger, / endowed with all sovereignty, they were completely free of all diseases.
By the grace of that god, human beings at that time / became immortal and ageless, endowed with wealth and grain.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, mortals were adorned with sons and grandsons. / Thus, O fortunate one, at the doorways of their houses constantly
stood most holy wish-fulfilling trees, bestowing the fruit of all desires, / cows that milk every wish, and wish-granting gems.
They were present in their holy homes, granting every wish. / Humans became immortal, adorned with sons and grandsons.
They were rid of all faults, solely by the grace of Viṣṇu, / endowed with all good fortune, and possessed of holy auspiciousness.
Endowed with pure gifts, devoted to knowledge and meditation, / among men there was neither famine, nor disease, nor untimely death.
While that righteous king Yayāti ruled at that time, / all men were Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
Fixing their meditation on him, absorbed in him, all became intent on [his] devotional sentiment. / Their dwellings were divine and sacred, O best of the twice-born,
furnished with bright white flags and conches; / with banners bearing the mace, and constantly marked with the discus,
and marked with the lotus, they shone like heavenly chariots; / their houses had their wall surfaces painted with beautiful pictures.
Everywhere at the doorways of the houses, in sacred places, O best ones, / were divine groves and auspicious verdant lawns.
And with tulasī, O best of the twice-born, and with temples of Keśava in them, / the holy, divine houses of living beings shone constantly.
Everywhere the auspicious Vaiṣṇava devotion was widely seen, / and conch sounds on earth with reverberating blasts, O friend,
were heard there, O chief of Brahmins, destroying faults and sins. / Conches, svastikas, and lotuses on the doorways and walls of houses
were painted by women through devotion to Viṣṇu, O best of the twice-born, / with melodious songs, beautiful tunes, modulations, notes, and sweet voices.
Devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu, people sang of Keśava.
With love they spoke of Hari, Murāri, and Keśava; others of the invincible Mādhava, / of the glorious Narasiṃha, the lotus-eyed one, Govinda, the sole lord of Kamalā;
they chanted Kṛṣṇa, the shelter, the refuge, and worshiped Rāma with repetitions; / those foremost Vaiṣṇavas bowed down to Viṣṇu with prostrations, absorbed in his meditation.

2.75.m: Sukarma said: / [Calling upon] Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Rāma, Mukunda, Madhusūdana, / Nārāyaṇa, the form of Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Acyuta,
Keśava, Padmanābha, Vāsudeva, and Vāmana, / the Boar, the Tortoise, the Fish, Hṛṣīkeśa, the sovereign of gods,
the Lord of the universe, the Universal-formed, the Infinite, sinless, pure, / the Supreme Person, the lotus-eyed, Śrīdhara, Śrīpati, Hari,
Śrīnivāsa, the yellow-robed, Mādhava, the giver of liberation, the Lord— / thus indeed human beings constantly recited [his] names.
All men—the young, the old, and young maidens— / and women, constantly engaged in household chores, sang sweetly of Hari.
While sitting, lying down, moving about, meditating, and speaking, [they called on] Mādhava; / while playing, even children bowed to Govinda.
Day and night they spoke the most sweet name of Hari, / and the utterance of [the name of] Viṣṇu was heard everywhere, O best of the twice-born.
Mortals dwelt on the surface of the earth by the power of the Vaiṣṇava [religion]. / On the pinnacles of mansions, on pitchers, and in shrines of the gods,
disci shone like the disks of the sun. / The condition that is seen in Vaikuṇṭha was that which existed on the surface of the earth.
Merit was made by that great-souled king, O Brahmin, / and the earth's surface was thus brought to equality with Viṣṇu's world.
By Yayāti, the Vaiṣṇava son of Nahuṣa, / the surface of the earth was unified with the condition of both worlds.
No difference at all was seen between the earth's surface and Viṣṇu's [abode]. / Just as Vaiṣṇavas utter Viṣṇu's name in Vaikuṇṭha,
so human beings uttered it on the surface of the earth. / A single state was seen, O Brahmin, in both worlds.
There was no fear of old age or sickness; men were free from death; / and an abundance of gifts and enjoyments was seen on earth.
Men enjoyed the holy happiness from sons and greater [joy] from grandsons; / humans on earth enjoyed [them] with happiness, O best one.
Through the bestowal of Viṣṇu's grace and through his teaching, / human beings were always Vaiṣṇavas, freed from all afflictions.
The majesty of heaven was brought onto the earth's surface by the king / for a duration of twenty-five years, O best of kings.
All men were free from disease, devoted to knowledge and meditation, / all intent on sacrifice and generosity, and human beings possessed compassionate dispositions.
Devoted to helping others, holy, blessed, they were recipients of renown; / all were intent on dharma, O Brahmin, devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu.
Instructed by that king, they became Vaiṣṇavas on earth. / Viṣṇu said: Hear, O tiger among kings, the deeds of that monarch.
Nāhuṣa was always devoted to all dharma and a devotee of Viṣṇu. / A hundred thousand years thus passed for him on earth.
His body appeared fresh, like that of a twenty-five-year-old; / he shone then in beauty and youth like a twenty-five-year-old,
powerful, full of maturity, by the grace of that wielder of the discus. / Abiding on earth, those humans did not go to Yama at all.
Freed from attachment and aversion, free from the snares of affliction, / happy through gifts and merit, devoted to all duties,
all those people, O king, expanded with their lineage, / just as dūrvā grass and banyan trees spread on the earth's surface.
Just as all those humans multiplied through sons and grandsons, / free from the fault of death, those people lived long indeed.
With firm bodies and happy, free from old age and sickness, / all men on the surface of the earth appeared as twenty-five-year-olds.
All were devoted to truthful conduct, devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu; / thus all those mortals, by the grace of that wielder of the discus,
all humans became devoted to generosity and enjoyment. / No mortal at all was heard of as dead in the world, O best of men.
They saw no sorrow, and entered into no sin. / Whatever was the form of heaven, such became the form of the earth's surface,
it became so, O best of men, by the grace of that wielder of the discus. / The messengers of Yama were driven off, beaten by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
Weeping, all of them went to Dharmarāja and told one another. / All that conduct of the king was related by those messengers:
"The earthly realm has become deathless through the enjoyment of charity under the Sun, / and it was made so, O god, by Nahuṣa's son, Yayāti.
By that holy devotee of Viṣṇu, it has been shown to have the form of heaven." / All this was then heard by Dharmarāja.
Dharmarāja, having then heard the full account from his messengers there, / contemplated the whole matter after hearing of the king's deed in this way.

2.76.m: Sukarma said: / That son of Sūrya went to heaven together with all the messengers / to see the thousand-eyed [Indra] there, surrounded by hosts of gods.
The king of the gods then saw Dharmarāja arriving; / rising up in haste, he gave him supreme water offering,
and asked of his coming: "Relate it before me." / Having heard that great speech uttered by the king of the gods,
Dharmarāja told all the great deeds of Yayāti. / Dharmarāja said: / "Listen, O lord of the gods, to the reason for my coming.
I will tell here the reason why I have come to you. / By the great-souled son of Nahuṣa, who is devoted to Viṣṇu,
all mortals who live on the earth have been made Vaiṣṇavas. / The form of the mortal world has indeed been made equal to Vaikuṇṭha.
Men have become immortal, freed from old age and disease. / They do not commit any sin, nor do they speak untruth.
They are devoid of desire and anger, freed from greed and delusion, / inclined to charity, high-souled, and all devoted to dharma.
With all acts of dharma they worship flawless Nārāyaṇa. / By means of that Vaiṣṇava dharma, men on the face of the earth
are healthy, free from sorrow, and all have enduring youth. / Just as dūrvā grass and banyan trees spread over the earth, O god,
In this way they multiplied with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons; / and with their sons and great-grandsons, they passed from lineage to lineage.
Thus, indeed, the entire mortal world has been made Vaiṣṇava, / freed from old age and death, by that son of Nahuṣa.
I have fallen from my post and have been deprived of my occupation. / All this has been described—the destruction of my duty.
Knowing this, O thousand-eyed one, act for the benefit of this world. / All this has been told to you, as I was questioned by you.
For this reason, O Indra, I have come into your presence." / Indra said: / "Previously a messenger was sent by me to summon that great-souled one,
O lord Dharmarāja, and it was said by him to the messenger: / 'I have no desire for the pleasures of heaven, nor will I go to heaven again.
I will make the entire orb of the earth resemble heaven.' / Thus spoke that king; he protects his subjects.
By the power of his dharma, I remain ever afraid." / Dharma said: / "By some means or other, bring that good king here,
O fortunate king of the gods, if you wish to please me." / Hearing those words of Dharma, the ruler of the gods,
intelligent as he was, pondered deeply, O king. / Calling Kāmadeva and the Gandharvas, Purandara,
the high-minded god, brought Makaranda and Rati, [saying]: / "You must act in such a way that the king comes [here].
Go to the earthly realm, commanded by me, without a doubt." / Kāma said: / "I shall perform what is pleasing and beneficial to both of you, without a doubt.
Watch me and the king stationed in the encounter!" / Saying "So be it," they all went to where that king, the son of Nahuṣa, was.
In the form of actors, Kāma and the others acted with their craft, O twice-born; / greeting him with blessings, they announced an excellent play.
Hearing their words, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, / wise as he was, arranged an assembly of learned men, resembling that of the gods.
The king himself, skilled in knowledge and worldly wisdom, arrived. / While the king, that son of Nahuṣa, was watching their play,
depicting the deeds of Vāmana and his birth in the form of a brāhmaṇa, / [there was] an incomparable [woman] in the world, singing an excellent song in a sweet voice.
Old age, O king, singing then in the form of an Arya woman, / by the charm of her song and her graceful smile,
by her sweet conversation and by the illusion of Kandarpa, / bewildered him with that emotion and that divine performance.
As was the form of Bali and of Vindhyāvalī formerly, / and as was the form of Vāmana, so did Cupid make it.
Kāma himself was the stage manager, Spring was the assistant, / and that Rati, his cheerful beloved, took on the role of the actress.
Entering behind the scenes, O king, in that dance performance, / the highly wise Makaranda agitated the king.
The more the lord of the earth watched the excellent dance and heard the song, / the more that noble-minded [Kāma] bewitched the king through what the actress performed.

2.77.m: Sukarma said: / By Kāma's song, dance, and graceful laughter / in the guise of an actor, the king of kings was infatuated, O Pippala.
Having passed urine and feces, that king, the son of Nahuṣa, / sat upon his seat without washing his feet.
Finding that opportunity, old age entered the king. / By Kāma, O best of kings, Indra's beneficial work was accomplished.
When that play ended and they had departed, the king, / though righteous in nature, was overcome by old age, his mind attached to desire.
Bewildered by the delusion of lust, agitated, his senses impaired, / the righteous-minded one became utterly infatuated and carried away by sensual objects.
One day, the king, afflicted by the addiction to hunting, / went into the forest and played there, fallen under the sway of delusion and passion.
While the high-souled king was sporting with delight, / a single, peerless deer with four horns approached.
Beautiful in all its limbs, O king, with hair of gold and silver, / with limbs variegated like the light of jewels, lovely and captivating to the mind.
He ran swiftly, holding a bow with arrow in hand; / the intelligent one thought, "Some demon has arrived!"
The king was drawn far away by that deer; / going with the speed of his chariot, he became exhausted by fatigue.
Even as he watched, the deer vanished. / He saw a forest there, wonderful and comparable to Nandana,
filled with lovely trees, adorned with the five elements, / with heavy, sacred sandalwoods, graced with clusters of plantains,
with bakula, aśoka, punnāga, coconut, and tinduka trees, / with areca nuts, dates, kumudas, and saptaparṇa trees,
with blossoming karṇikāras and various trees bearing fruit in all seasons, / and then with ketakas and pāṭalas endowed with the fragrance of flowers.
Looking around, O great king, he saw an excellent lake, / filled with holy water and five yojanas in extent,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, resounding with water-birds, / delighted with lotuses and shining with white water-lilies.
shining with red water-lilies, adorned with golden lotuses, / illuminated with blue water-lilies, and greatly embellished with white lotuses;
resounding everywhere with intoxicated honey-bees; / thus he saw the supreme lake, endowed with all excellences,
five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long, / an auspicious pool on all sides, adorned with heavenly qualities.
Exhausted by the speed of the chariot and somewhat afflicted by fatigue, / he sat down on its bank under the very cool shade of a mango tree.
Having bathed and drunk the cold water, fragrant with the scent of lotuses, / which allayed all weariness and was like nectar itself,
as the king sat in the shade of that tree, / he heard the sound of singing just as it was being sung.
As a celestial woman sings, so was this sound heard. / The great king, fond of song, fell into profound contemplation.
While the righteous-souled one, filled with wonder, pondered for a moment, / there came an excellent woman with plump hips and breasts.
As the king watched, she approached in that forest, / her limbs adorned with all ornaments, rich in virtuous nature and auspicious marks.
She arrived in that forest and stood before the king. / The great king said to her: "Who are you, and to whom do you belong?
For what purpose have you come? Tell me the reason for that." / Questioned by him, O Pippala, she said nothing at all,
whether good or bad, in reply to the protector of the earth. The fair-faced lady / merely laughed and went away swiftly, a slender woman with the neck of a vīṇā in her hand.
Then the lord of kings was overcome by great astonishment: / "Addressed by me, she did not even utter an answer to me."
Yayāti, the lord of the earth, fell into thought once more: / "The golden deer with four horns that was seen by me—
from that, a woman arose; that seems true to me. / Surely this will be an illusory form of the Dānavas."
Having reflected for a moment, King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa— / while the king was still pondering, the woman in the great forest,
O brāhmaṇa, vanished, having laughed at the king's son. / In the meantime, that sweet-voiced song
was heard again, supremely divine, endowed with modulations and melodic expansions. / The king went quickly to where the great sound of singing was.
At the edge of the water there was an excellent thousand-petaled lotus, / and upon it was an excellent woman, endowed with good conduct, beauty, and virtues,
possessed of divine marks, adorned with celestial ornaments; / shining alone with heavenly graces, holding the neck of a vīṇā in her hand,
singing a song with a sweet voice, accompanied by rhythm, measure, and tempo; / and by the power of that singing, enchanting all moving and unmoving beings,
the gods, all the hosts of sages, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras. / Seeing that large-eyed woman, radiant with beauty and splendor—
for in the whole saṃsāra, among moving and unmoving beings, there was no other woman like her— / just as earlier, an actor entering old age, upon entering the king's body,
great desire was stirred, and then became manifest in him; / just as fire, touching clarified butter, becomes blazing with rays,
even so, seeing her, desire became manifest from his body. / With his mind possessed by the god of love upon seeing that lovely-eyed woman,
[he thought:] "I have never seen a young woman of such form, who enchants the universe!" / Reflecting for a moment, the king, his mind clinging to desire,
and yearning for her because of separation, was then seized by longing; / burning with the fire of passion, afflicted by the fever of love:
"How may she become mine? How will her affection arise, / so that this young maiden, lotus-faced and lotus-eyed, embraces me?
If she is attained, then my life would be fruitful!" / Having thus reflected, the righteous Yayāti, the lord of the earth,
said to the shapely woman: "Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O auspicious one? / The woman who was seen previously has been seen again.
That righteous one asked her: "And who is this woman at your side? / Tell me everything, O blessed one; I am indeed the son of Nahuṣa,
born in the Lunar dynasty, the lord of the seven continents, O fair lady; / Yayāti is my name, O goddess, famed in the three worlds.
My heart longs deeply for union with you; / grant me union, O auspicious lady, and do what is exceedingly dear [to me].
Whatever you desire, O blessed one, that I shall give, there is no doubt. / I have been struck down by unconquerable passion, O fair-complexioned lady.
Therefore protect me, who am wretched and have fled to you for refuge. / My kingdom, the entire earth, and even my own body,
I will give to you in exchange for union with you; even these three worlds [I give] to you." / Hearing the words of that king, the woman whose face resembled a lotus
said to Viśālā, her female friend: "Speak to the king who has arrived, / and [tell him] my name, place of origin, father, and mother, O fair lady,
and also declare before him my single-minded affection." / Knowing her desire, Viśālā then said to the lord of the earth
in sweet words: "Listen, O son of the king! / Viśālā said: Kāma was burned long ago by the god of gods, Śambhu.
Deprived of her husband, Rati wept sweetly out of sorrow. / In this very lake, O best of kings, that Rati then resided.
Hearing her lamentation, which was so sweet and full of pathos, / the gods then became filled with supreme compassion,
O king of kings, and spoke these words to Śaṅkara: / 'Revive Manobhava once again, O Mahādeva!
What will become of this wretched, fortunate lady without her husband? / Bring her together with Kāma, out of affection for us!'
Hearing their words, he said: 'I shall revive Manobhava. / Though devoid of a body, this five-arrowed Manobhava
will undoubtedly become the friend of Mādhava again; / he shall live with a divine body, not otherwise.'
And by the grace of Mahādeva, the fish-bannered god was brought back to life. / Comforting the goddess's Kāma with blessings in this manner, O best of men,
[Śiva said:] 'Go, Kāma, and live always with your beloved!' / Thus spoke the exceedingly splendid one, who causes maintenance and destruction.
Then Kāma reached the lake where the sorrowful Rati was staying. / This is Kāmasaras, O king, where Rati resided securely.
When the mind-born god was burned, O fortunate one, overcome with grief / from Rati's anger, a fire of terrible form was born.
Extremely burned even by that, Rati, fainting in delusion, / shed a flood of tears, deprived of her husband, O best of men.
The tear-drops fell from her eyes into the water. / From them arose Great Grief, the destroyer of all happiness.
Thereafter Old Age arose from the tears, O best of kings. / From them was born the evil-minded Separation, the destroyer.
Both Sorrow and Burning Agony were born then, terrible ones. / Then was born Fainting, dreadful, destroying happiness.
From Grief were born, O great king, the Fever of Love and Confusion, / Lamentation, Bewilderment, Madness, and Death itself.
From her tear-drops were born these destroyers of the universe; / at Rati's side they all arose, bearing bodies of affliction,
embodied, O great king, endowed with true-natured qualities. / 'Here Kāma has arrived!'—someone said then, O king.
Filled with great joy upon seeing Kāma arrive, / from her eyes filled with tears, drops of tears fell.
In the midst of the waters, O great king, creatures were born out of fickleness. / Then Prīti was born, and Khyāti and Lajjā, O best of men.
From them arose Mahānanda, and another [daughter], Śānti, O best of kings. / Two auspicious maidens were born who bestow the pleasure of enjoyment.
Play, sport, amorous mood, and union were great indeed, O king. / But from the left eye of Rati, tears fell out of joy.
They fell upon the water, O king, and from that a beautiful lotus was born. / From that beautiful lotus this woman of lovely face was born.
Named Aśrubindumatī, she is the daughter of Rati, O best of men. / Out of love for her, bringing her happiness, I always remain near her.
By the nature of friendship, I am always delighted and auspicious. / My well-known name is Viśālā; I am the daughter of Varuṇa, O king.
I attend beside her, and out of affection I am always loving. / All this concerning her and concerning myself has been told to you.
Desiring a husband, the lovely-faced maiden practiced austerities, O king of kings.” / The king said: “Everything has been told by you, and I have understood it, auspicious one. Listen:
Let this fair-faced daughter of Rati indeed accept me! / Whatever this young woman desires, all that I shall give.
Act in such a way, fortunate one, that she comes under my power.” / Viśālā said: “I shall declare her vow; listen to it, O protector of the earth:
A man endowed with youth, all-knowing, marked with the signs of a hero, / equal to the king of the gods, O king, endowed with conduct aligned with dharma,
splendid, very wise, generous, best among sacrificers, / a knower of virtues and of the nature of dharma, a vessel of merit,
equal to the lord of the world, O king, intent upon dharma through well-performed sacrifices, / endowed with all sovereign power, like a second Nārāyaṇa,
always very dear to the gods, extremely dear to the brāhmaṇas, / devoted to brāhmaṇas, knowing the reality of the Vedas, renowned for valor in the three worlds—
endowed with such qualities, venerated by the three worlds, / wise, very dear, and handsome—such a choice husband she desires in her heart.”
Yayāti said: / “Know that I have arrived here endowed with such qualities! / I am a fitting husband for her, created by the Creator, without doubt.”
Viśālā said: / “I know you to be augmented with merit in the three worlds, O king. / All the qualities previously spoken by me exist in you.
Yet because of a single flaw she does not accept you. / This doubt has arisen in me, though you are filled with Viṣṇu, O king.”
Yayāti said: / “Tell me truly the great flaw because of which she does not approve, / O you of beautiful limbs! Show favor, fair-faced one!”
Viśālā said: / “Why do you not know your own flaw, O lord of the earth? / Your body is pervaded by old age; because of this she does not accept [you].”
Hearing this terrible and unpleasant speech, the lord of the earth, / filled with great sorrow, the king spoke to her again:
“The flaw of old age is not mine, gentle lady; never has it arisen on my body / through contact with anything. Indeed, I do not know the coming of that old age!
Whatever she desires that is difficult to obtain in the three worlds, auspicious one, / that I wish to give her. Let the best boon be chosen.”
Viśālā said: / “When you become free from old age, then you will be very dear to her. / This is certain, O king; I speak the truth, the truth.
The sacred revelation speaks thus, O king: if old age is transferred / to a son, a brother, or a servant, it moves over into his body.
Taking his youth and giving him old age in return, / an auspicious agreement of affection arises between the two with pleasant consent.
Just as one who gives the merit of his own gift out of compassion, / that fruit becomes his, O king, of this there is no doubt.
When merit acquired with hardship is given to another, / that becomes great merit for him, and he enjoys the fruit of merit.
Let [old age] be given to a son, O king, and taking youth from him, / return here in beauty, O protector of the earth.
Whenever you wish to enjoy, do so then, O protector of the earth.” / Having spoken thus to the king, Viśālā ceased.
Sukarma said: / Having heard this, the king of kings then spoke to Viśālā. / The king said: “So be it, highly fortunate one, I shall do your bidding.”
Attached to passion and utterly bewildered, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, / went home, summoned his sons, and spoke these words:
The king [summoned] Turu, Pūru, Kuru, and Yadu, who loved his father: / “O dear sons, make me happy by my command!”
The sons said: / “A father's word must be carried out by sons, whether auspicious or inauspicious. / Speak quickly, father! Know it to be done without doubt.”
Hearing that speech of his sons, the lord of the earth / declared to them again, his mind agitated with joy:

2.78.m: Yayāti said: / “Let my sorrow-giving old age be taken by one steadfast among you, my sons, / and let your youth be given to me,
for this excellent form is your own, O fortunate ones. / Today my mind is tormented, attached to a woman, and exceedingly fickle.
Just as fire churns water standing in a vessel, / so the fire of passion, O sons, has stirred up my mind.
Let one of you, my sons, take my sorrow-bestowing old age / and give his own youth, so that I may roam at will.
The best son who will remove my old age / shall enjoy the kingdom with me and bear the lineage and the bow.
Happiness, abundant prosperity, wealth, and grain shall be his; / his offspring shall be vast, and his fame and renown shall endure.”
The sons said: / “You are devoted to dharma, O king, and protect the subjects with truth. / Why has such a state of mind arisen in you, fickle by nature?”
The king said: / “Dancers previously came to my city and danced; / from them arose my infatuation with desire, and such delusion occurred.
My body is overcome with old age, but my mind is possessed by love. / I have become completely agitated by passion, O best of sons!
A certain woman of divine form and lovely face was seen by me. / She was addressed by me, O sons, but the chaste maiden said nothing to me.
Her friend, beautiful and discerning, named Viśālā, / spoke an auspicious word to me that bestows my happiness:
‘When you become free from old age, then you will be very dear to her.’ / Accepting the words spoken by her, I have come home.
This has been declared by me for the purpose of removing old age. / Knowing this, my good sons, my happiness must indeed be brought about.”
Turu said: / “The body is obtained by sons through the grace of father and mother, / and dharma is performed, O king, by the wise one through the body.
Service to parents is to be performed by sons, especially so; / yet this is not the time for the giving of youth, O lord of men.
Sensory pleasure should be enjoyed by men in the first stage of life, O king; / now is not that time present for you at this moment.
Having given old age, father, that has reached an advanced state, to a son, / happiness is to be enjoyed afterwards, but your life may not remain!
Therefore, O great king, I will not carry out your word.” / Thus spoke Turu, the eldest son, to the king at that time.
Hearing those words of Turu, the king became enraged; / the righteous one, his eyes reddened with fury, cursed Turu:
"You have flouted this command of mine, O evil-minded one! / Therefore become a sinner, cast out from all dharmas!
Deprived of the topknot and devoid of the Veda and the treatises, / you will undoubtedly be bereft of all right conduct!
A killer of brāhmaṇas, hateful to the gods, a wine-drinker, devoid of truth, / a performer of cruel deeds, you shall become the lowest of men!
Clinging to liquor, hungry, sinful, you shall be a cow-killer, / suffering from skin disease, unfastened in dress, an enemy of brāhmaṇas, neglected,
an adulterer with the wives of others, terribly fierce, a debauchee, / eating everything, and always foolish in mind!
You shall take pleasure with a woman of your own gotra, a destroyer of all righteousness, / your self bereft of virtue and knowledge, and afflicted with leprosy!
Your sons and grandsons will undoubtedly become / such as this: destroyers of all merit, Mlecchas, thoroughly defiled!"
Having thus cursed Turu severely, he then spoke to his son Yadu: / "Take on my old age here, and enjoy an unobstructed kingdom!"
Folding his hands in supplication, Yadu said to the king: / Yadu said: "I cannot bear the burden of old age, father; have mercy!
Cold, travelling on foot, bad food, aging women, / and adversity of the mind: these are the five causes of old age.
I cannot endure the suffering of old age in my youth, O king! / For who is able to bear it? Forgive me now!"
Enraged, the great king cursed Yadu, O delight of the twice-born: / "Your lineage will never be fit for kingship!
Bereft of strength, splendour, and forbearance, devoid of the duty of a kṣatriya, / it will undoubtedly turn its back on my command!"
Yadu said: "I am blameless, O great king; why have I been cursed by you now? / Have pity on a wretched one; show a gracious countenance!"
The king said: "Mahādeva will indeed produce an emanation through his own portion in your family, my son; / then your lineage shall be purified."
Yadu said: "I am your son, O great king, blameless and yet cursed by you; / let favor be shown to me, if compassion exists within you!"
The king said: "He who would be the eldest son is one who removes his father's sorrow; / he enjoys the inheritance of the kingdom, and he must bear the burden.
You did not practice dharma; you are undoubtedly unworthy of being addressed! / By you, my order has been broken—slayers [of commands] deserve great punishment!
Therefore there is no favor; do as you please!" / Yadu said: "Since my kingdom, family, and beauty have been ruined by you, O king,
therefore I shall become wicked, O master of your lineage, O king! / In your lineage there will be various divisions of kṣatriyas;
their villages and prosperous regions, and whatever women and jewels there are, / will undoubtedly be enjoyed by the most fierce and mighty
Turuṣkas born of my lineage, taking the form of Mlecchas, / because all [of mine] were ruined and cursed by you with very terrible curses!"
Thus the enraged Yadu spoke to the king, O best of monarchs; / then, enraged, the great king cursed him again in this manner:
"Hear this! All those born in your line who destroy my subjects, / as long as the moon and the sun, the earth and the constellations and stars exist,
for so long shall those Mlecchas be boiled in the hells Kumbhīpāka and Raurava!" / Then, seeing the young child Kuru playing, endowed with auspicious marks,
the king did not call him, his son, the prince; / knowing him to be a child, he abandoned Kuru at that time.
Summoning that virtuous Pūru, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, / the lord of the world spoke: "Take my old age once more!
Enjoy the kingdom given by me, very holy and freed of obstacles!" / Pūru said: "The kingdom should be enjoyed by your Majesty, just as it was enjoyed by your father.
I will carry out your command; let your old age be given to me, O king! / Becoming endowed with lovely form today through my youth,
enjoy pleasures with auspicious deeds, with your mind devoted to sensual objects; / roam about with her as long as you wish, O fortunate one!
As long as I live, father, for that long shall I bear the old age!" / Being addressed in this way even by his son Pūru, the lord of the earth,
overcome with great joy, replied to that son: / "Since, my child, you have not broken my command here, but executed it,
therefore I will bestow upon you that which gives abundant happiness! / Since my old age has been taken and your own youth given,
by that rule over the kingdom given by me, O wise one!" / Thus addressed by that king, O ruler of the earth, virtuous Pūru
gave him his youth and took the old age from him, O king; / then, when the exchange of age had been made between father and son,
Pūru appeared older in all his limbs than he had been, / while the king attained freshness, like a youth of sixteen years.
Endowed with immense beauty, he was like a second Manmatha. / The bow, the kingdom, the parasol, the fan, the throne, the elephant,
the treasury, the realm, the entire army, the chowrie, and the chariot— / thus the great king gave all to that high-souled Pūru.
Enamoured of love and righteous, the son of Nahuṣa, thinking of that woman, / went with swift strides to that lake known as Kāmākhya, like an ocean,
where Aśrubindumatī was. / Seeing that large-eyed woman with lovely and swelling breasts,
the great king, his mind captivated by love, said to Viśālā: / The king said: "I have arrived, O fortunate one, O Viśālā of lovely eyes!
Old age has been abandoned, O blessed one, and I am endowed with youth; / having become a youth, I have arrived; let her now become mine!
Whatever she desires, I will give that to her without doubt." / Viśālā said: "Although you have come, having cast off vile old age,
you are tainted by one fault; she will not accept you." / The king said: "Tell me my fault, if you know it for certain;
I will certainly abandon that fault, transforming it into virtue, without doubt."

2.79.m: Viśālā said: "For him whose wives are Śarmiṣṭhā and fair-faced Devayānī, / good fortune is indeed seen there; otherwise it is not so, O king.
Then how could you, O fortunate one, become subject to her wishes? / You are established as a husband with the sentiment born of having co-wives!
You are with serpents, O great king, just like a sandalwood tree on the earth; / for a great sandalwood tree is indeed surrounded by serpents, O king.
In the same way, you are surrounded by serpents named co-wives! / Better is entering into fire; better is falling from the top of a mountain peak,
[than] a beloved who is endowed with beauty and lustre, yet accompanied by a co-wife; / such a beloved, mingled with the poison of a co-wife, is not preferable.
Therefore, she does not accept you, an ocean of virtues, as her lover." / The king said: "I have no business with Devayānī, nor with Śarmiṣṭhā, O fair-faced one!
“Therefore behold my treasury, filled with the quality of goodness and righteousness.” / Aśrubindumatī said: “I am the enjoyer of your kingdom and of your body, O king.
“Whatever I say, O king, that must certainly be done by you. / For this purpose, give me your hand, O lover of dharma,
endowed with much dharma, possessed of fair characteristics.” / The king said: “I will not take any other wife but you, O fair-complexioned lady.
Enjoy the kingdom, the entire earth, and my body, O lovely-faced one, / along with the treasury, O fair-limbed lady; here is my hand given to you.
Whatever you say, gentle lady, that alone indeed I shall do.” / Aśrubindumatī said: “By this, O fortunate one, I become your wife.”
Having heard this, the king of kings, his eyes filled with joy, / King Yayāti, [took her] by the gāndharva marriage.
He wed the virtuous daughter of Manmatha, O best of men; / along with her, the great-souled prince revelled
on the shores of the ocean, in forests and in gardens, / on charming mountains, and by rivers with her.
The king of kings, the sovereign of the earth, sported in the prime of youth; / thus twenty thousand [years] passed for him as he was devoted [to pleasure]—
for that great-souled king Yayāti, O king of kings. / Viṣṇu said: In this manner the great king Yayāti was then enchanted by her,
through the deceit of Kandarpa, for the sake of Indra, O wise one. / Sukarma said: Thus, O Pippala, that king Yayāti, lord of the earth,
infatuated by the daughter of Kāma through her charming desire / and lovely lovemaking, did not know day from night.
Once, that fair-eyed daughter of Kāma addressed the king / Yayāti, who was infatuated, bowed low, submissive, and subject to her control.
Aśrubindumatī said: “A craving has arisen in me, beloved; fulfill this desire of mine: / perform an aśvamedha, the best of sacrifices, O lord of the earth.”
The king said: “So be it, O illustrious lady; I shall do what is most pleasing to you.” / Having summoned his best son, who was free of desire for royal enjoyment,
who, being called, had come, his neck bowed in devotion, / and having folded his hands, then offered his salutation.
He then bowed to her feet, his neck bowed in devotion: / “Let an order be given, O king, on account of which I was called and have come.
What shall I do, O fortunate one? I am your servant and have bowed down.” / The king said: “O son, prepare the equipment for the aśvamedha sacrifice,
having summoned the holy twice-born, the officiating priests, and the rulers of the earth.” / Being thus addressed, the most righteous Pūru, endowed with great splendor,
carried out everything completely, just as was said by the great-souled one. / Along with that daughter of Kāma, he took the excellent consecration.
Having given manifold gifts in the sacrificial enclosure of the aśvamedha / to the brāhmaṇas, O great king, endless and abundant gifts,
and especially to the poor, King Yayāti, / at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the great king said to that fair-faced lady:
“What else very pleasing to you shall I do, O girl? Tell me; / I shall accomplish all that, O goddess, whether possible or impossible, O lovely-faced one.”
Sukarma said: Thus addressed by that king, she spoke in reply to the sovereign: / “A craving has arisen in me, O sinless king; fulfill it for me.
The world of Indra, the world of Brahmā, and likewise the world of Śiva, / and the world of Viṣṇu, O great king—I desire to see what is most delightful.
Show them to me, O fortunate one, if I am very dear to you.” / Being thus addressed by her, the king spoke to that beloved woman:
“Well said, well said, O woman of shapely hips! You speak of a meritorious thing indeed, / but out of a woman's nature, fickleness, and curiosity, O lovely-faced one,
what has been spoken by you, O fortunate one, seems impossible to me. / That is to be achieved by the giving of merit, by sacrifice, and by austerity;
otherwise it cannot be achieved, that which has been spoken by you, O lovely-faced one. / Yet an impossible thing, mingled with merit, has indeed been spoken by you.
No mortal from the world of mortals, even one of great virtuous deeds, / has ever been seen or heard by me to have gone to heaven with this physical body.
Therefore, O woman of shapely hips, what has been spoken by you to me is impossible; / I will do something else pleasing to you—speak of that, my beloved.”
The lady said: “It may indeed be impossible for other men, O king, without a doubt; / but it is possible for you, O great king: I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
In austerity, in renown, in warrior deeds, in gifts, and in sacrifices, O lord of the earth, / there is no other human being like you in the mortal world.
Warrior strength and supreme splendor are all established in you; / therefore, you must fulfill what is pleasing to me, O son of Nahuṣa.”

2.80.m: Pippala said: “When the king wed the daughter of Kāma, O best of the twice-born, / what did those two previous, highly virtuous wives do then—
the illustrious Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan? / Recount all of their conduct before me.”
Sukarma said: When the daughter of Kāma was brought to his own house by that king, / the high-minded Devayānī rivalled her exceedingly.
For her sake, her own two sons were cursed, their minds agitated by rage; / and summoning Śarmiṣṭhā, the renowned woman cried out.
In beauty, splendor, gifts, truth, and pious vows, / both Śarmiṣṭhā and Devayānī rivalled with her.
And the daughter of Kāma knew their malicious intent; / she immediately recounted everything to the king here, O brāhmaṇa.
Then the great king, being enraged, summoned Yadu and said: / “Go, let Śarmiṣṭhā be killed, and also the daughter of Śukra.
Do what is pleasing to me, my son, if you consider what is truly good.” / Having thus heard that command of his father, Yadu then
spoke in reply to that king of kings, his father, O honor-giving one: / “I will not kill the two mothers, father, since they are free from fault.
A great fault in killing a mother is declared by scholars of the Veda; / therefore, O great king, I will not commit the murder of these two.
Even when a mother might be smeared with a thousand faults, / or a sister, O great king, or likewise a daughter,
she should never be killed by sons or by brothers. / Knowing this, O great king, I will not kill the two mothers.”
Hearing the words of Yadu, the king indeed became enraged; / King Yayāti, lord of the earth, then cursed his son:
“Since my command was transgressed by you today, you are like a sinner; / stained by my curse, partake of your mother's portion!”
Having spoken thus to his son Yadu, King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, / the illustrious great king, having cursed his son, along with her
revelled in happy enjoyment, intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu. / That fair-eyed Aśrubindumatī, lovely in all her limbs,
along with him enjoyed holy pleasures according to her heart's desire. / In this manner time passed for that great-souled Yayāti.
All his other subjects became undecaying and ageless; / all the people, O fortunate one, were intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu.
Through austerity, truthful disposition, and meditation upon Viṣṇu, O Pippala, / all the people were fortunate, happy, and servants of the virtuous.

2.81.m: Sukarma said: Just as that very wise Indra was always terrified of the great-souled / Yayāti, having seen his valor, gifts, abundant merits, and the like—

He dispatched the Apsaras Menakā on a messenger's mission:
"Go, auspicious, highly fortunate lady; proclaim my command!

Going from here to the daughter of Kāma, speak the King of the Gods' word:
'By whatever means possible, bring the king here.'"

Having heard this, Menakā, who was sent there, went
and reported everything that had been spoken by the King of the Gods.

Having been spoken to thus, Menakā, impelled by him, departed.
When Menakā had gone, the resolute daughter of Rati,

the renowned lady, said to the king, the embodiment of dharma:
"O King, formerly I was brought [here] by you with a true vow;

your own hand was given into [mine], and I was taken into your house.
Whatever I speak, O King, that very deed must indeed be done by you.

If my word is not acted upon by you in this way, O hero,
I shall abandon you and go to my father's house."

The king said:
"Whatever was spoken by you, auspicious lady, I will certainly do—there is no doubt.
Setting aside the impossible, tell me what is possible, O goddess."

Aśrubindumatī said:
"For this purpose, O lord of the earth, you were chosen by me here—
endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of all dharma,

knowing that everything is achievable [for you], the upholder of all,
the doer of all virtues, the creator of meritorious deeds,

knowing [you] to be the conqueror of the three worlds and peerless in the three worlds.
I know you to be a devotee of Viṣṇu, the greatest among the Vaiṣṇavas.
With this expectation you were accepted by me formerly as my husband. / He who has the grace of Viṣṇu may wander everywhere.”

Nothing is unobtainable, O best of kings, in the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings;
in all worlds indeed [influence] exists for you, O man of virtuous vows.

By the grace of Viṣṇu, you have the highest passage through the sky.
Having approached the mortal world, by you alone, O lord of the earth,

people have been made free from old age and gray hair, and free from death.
At all the doorsteps of mortals, O bull among men,

numerous wish-granting trees have been provided by you alone.
In the houses of mortals, the sages [and] wish-yielding cows

were sent by you, O King, and made to stay constantly;
and human beings were made happy with all desires by you.

Within a single household, thousands of noble people are seen;
in this way, the proliferation of the lineage of mortals was accomplished by you.

Even in defiance of Yama and Indra, O best of men,
the mortal world was made free of disease and sin by you.

By your own brilliance and self-regard, the surface of the earth was turned into heaven
and displayed [as such], O great king; there is no king equal to you.

No man like you has ever been born, nor will one ever arise.
I know you to be such a one, the illuminating sun of all virtues.

Therefore you were made my husband. Speak thus before me!
Setting aside jest, O lord of kings, speak the truth before me:

If truth is in you here, if dharma is in you, O lord of men,
[how can you say:] 'I have no supreme course in the celestial worlds or in the sky'?

And if, abandoning truth, you do not go to heaven,
then your word will become false; of this there is no doubt.

Whatever good was previously performed will be reduced to ashes."
The king said:
"You have spoken the truth, auspicious lady; for me there is neither possible nor impossible.

Everything is possible for me; every world is accessible through the good favor of the Lord of the Universe.
Why I am not going to heaven, O goddess, hear the single reason for that:

The gods will not allow me to return to the mortal world,
and then all my men, all my subjects, O fair-faced lady,

will be subject to death, bereft of me—there is no doubt.
I do not wish to go to heaven; I have spoken the truth, O fair-faced lady."

The queen said:
"Having seen those worlds, O great king, you will indeed return again.
Satisfy today this great, peerless desire that has arisen in me."

The king said:
"I shall do everything just as you have said, there is no doubt."
Having considered [this], the radiant Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa,

having spoken thus to his beloved, the king then reflected:
"Even a fish moving within the water is caught by a net;

even a deer with speed equal to the wind meets with bondage;
a bird sees meat situated a thousand leagues away,

yet, deluded by destiny, it does not see the snare around its neck.
Time produces equity and inequity; Time causes the loss of honor;

Time inflicts humiliation wherever one may abide;
it makes a man a giver, and then again a petitioner.

All beings, stationary and the rest, whether in heaven or on earth—
Time impels them all; Time alone indeed is this entire universe.

The Creator is without beginning or end, the supreme cause of the world;
Time ripens the worlds, just as a fruit upon a tree is brought to maturity.

Neither mantras, nor austerity, nor gifts, nor friends, nor relatives
are able to rescue a man afflicted by Time.

Three are the snares made by Time; they cannot be transcended:
marriage, birth, and death—when, where, and by whom.

Just as clouds in the sky are driven about by the wind,
so this universe is driven about by Time endowed with karma."

Calamities, injuries, defects, serpents, and diseases as well—
all these, appointed by karma, act upon a human being.

And whatever causes of happiness there are, means mixed with merit,
all those, connected with karma, would not perceive [only] good or evil.

Karma is the heir in this world; kinsmen are bound through karma;
and actions here impel a person toward pleasure and pain.

Just as gold or silver takes a definite shape,
so a living being, obedient to authority, is bound to its own karma.

These five are determined here for an embodied being while still in the womb:
life span, karma, wealth, learning, and death.

Just as an artisan makes whatever he desires from a lump of clay,
so previously performed karma follows after the agent.

The state of a deity, or human existence, the state of an animal, the condition of a bird,
subhuman birth, and stationary existence are all attained by one's own karmas.

He alone experiences that in that manner, as it was perpetually ordained by himself;
sorrow was ordained by oneself, and happiness was ordained by oneself.

Taking it from the bed of the womb, they experience what belongs to the previous body;
men never cast aside their own karma anywhere on earth.

Even if able through force or intellect to do otherwise,
they experience good deeds, and pains, and pleasures.

Having encountered a cause, a man is perpetually bound by the bonds of karma;
just as among a thousand cows a calf finds its mother,

so good and evil karma follows after the agent;
without experience of it, its destruction simply does not occur.

Who is capable of altering past bondage through karma?
Even as one runs exceedingly fast, destiny runs after him.

It sleeps with him while sleeping, as past karma was performed;
it stands beside him when standing, it follows him when walking.

It acts for him as he acts; it conforms like a shadow,
just as shadow and sunlight are ever closely linked to one another.
Just so are action and the doer closely bound to one another. / Planets, diseases, poisons, serpents, śākinīs, and rākṣasas,
torment a person afterwards who was already afflicted by past action. / By whomsoever, wherever happiness or even suffering is to be experienced,
he is brought there forcibly by fate, bound as if with a rope. / For fate is the master of living beings in bringing about happiness and suffering.
An action is planned in one way, whether awake or sleeping, / but wise fate intends to destroy it, [bringing it about] otherwise.
That which must be protected from weapons, fire, poison, and perils, it protects; / indeed, that which is unprotected remains so when thus protected by fate.
But for that which is destroyed by fate, no protection is seen. / Just as seeds sown in the earth, and wealth,
even so actions reside in the self and originate there. / Just as a lamp attains extinction from the exhaustion of oil,
so too a creature meets destruction from the body when its action is exhausted. / Thus death is proclaimed by the knowers of reality to arise from the exhaustion of action.
Various creatures and diseases are the causes of his death. / So too, this fruition of mine comes from what was done previously, not otherwise.
It has arrived without doubt; this one in a woman's form is without question [the cause]. / Where has my home arrived, with dramatic actors and dancers?
Through association with them, old age has settled upon my body. / I consider all that has been brought upon me to be certainly done by action.
Therefore action is primary, and remedies are useless. / Formerly, indeed, the king of the gods sent the best of messengers for my sake,
one named Mātali, but his word was not heeded. / The ripening of that action of mine is seen now.
Becoming absorbed in thought in this way, filled with great sorrow, [he thought]: / “If I do not lovingly fulfill her word by every means...”
both these, truth and dharma, will undoubtedly perish. / And that which is seen by my action has arrived as fitting.
It will happen without doubt, for fate is difficult to overcome.” / Having thus become engrossed in thought, King Yayāti
went for refuge to Kṛṣṇa, the God Hari, the remover of afflictions. / Having meditated upon, bowed to, and then praised Madhusūdana in his mind:
“Protect me, who have approached You for refuge, O Beloved of Kamalā!”

2.82.m: Sukarma said: / While the supreme, righteous king was thinking thus, / that goddess, the daughter of Rati with an exquisite face, said:
“Why do you ponder here in this way, O wise king? / For all women are generally fickle, without doubt.
I do not unsettle you out of fickleness. / I am certainly not having you leave your domain today, O best of kings,
as other women in the world, unchaste out of greed and delusion, / speak of what should not be done due to fickleness, O king of kings, O Indra [among men].
Faith has arisen in my heart only to see the worlds; / for sight of the gods is meritorious, and difficult even for good men to attain.
Tell me, O king, shall I bring about the sight of them? / If from association with me there should be any fault that produces sin,
you are pondering sorrow in this way like an ordinary person, / as if terrified by a great fear, as if fallen into the pit of delusion.
Cast off anxiety, O great king! You need not go to heaven. / That by which sorrow arises for you should never be done by me.”
Addressed thus, the king spoke to that lovely-faced woman: / “Hear now, O goddess, what was thought by me.
A loss of honor was not seen by me, nor that of one's own mind, O dear one. / When I have gone to heaven, my beloved, the subjects will be helpless.
The evil-minded Yama will terrify the subjects with diseases. / Together with you I shall depart to the heavenly world, O lovely-faced one.”
Having thus spoken to her, the king, summoning his excellent son / Pūru, who knew all dharma, who was wise and possessed of old age, [said:]
“Come, come, O knower of all dharma! You know dharma with certainty. / For by my command, O righteous one, dharma has been upheld by you.
Let my old age be returned, my dear, and take your youth back again. / Rule this kingdom of mine, along with treasury, army, and vehicles.
Enjoy the earth filled with jewels up to the ocean, / with villages, forests, and cities, given to you by me, O fortunate one.
The protection of subjects is meritorious and must always be performed, O sinless one. / The punishment of the wicked must ever be done, and the preservation of the virtuous.
And it must be performed by you, O child, according to the authority of the dharma treatises. / Of the brāhmaṇas, O fortunate one, according to rule and according to your duty,
protection must also be undertaken with devotion, since they are worthy of worship in the three worlds. / Every fifth or seventh day, examine the treasury, O wise one.
And the army must always be honored with favor, wealth, and food. / Have spies as your eyes, and be ever intent on giving.
Be restrained in counsel, which is always to be kept secret by the very learned. / Be self-controlled, and do not go hunting, my son.
Trust is to be placed in no one—among women, in the treasury, or in the great army. / You must make an assembly of worthy recipients and of all arts.
Worship Hṛṣīkeśa with sacrifices; be virtuous-minded at all times. / Crush all the thorns among the subjects day by day.
Bestow upon the subjects everything desired day by day. / The happiness of the subjects must be fostered; nourish the subjects, my dear son.
Propagate your own lineage; do not direct / wicked intention toward the wives of others or the wealth of others; follow the ancestors always.
Always reflect upon the Vedas, and ever upon the treatises; / act thus always, my child, and be dedicated to the practice of weapons.
Ever content, my child, be devoted to your own bed; / and always maintain the training of elephant, horse, and chariot.”
Thus instructing that son and congratulating him with blessings, / and having installed him with his own hand, he placed his weapon in his hand.
Taking back his own old age and giving him his youth, / King Yayāti then wished to go to heaven.

2.83.m: Sukarma said: / Having summoned all the subjects of the continents, the lord of the earth, / filled with great joy, spoke this word:
“To the realm of Indra, the realm of Brahmā, the realm of Rudra, and beyond that / the realm of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins and grants the destination to living beings,
I am going without doubt, together with this [maiden], O best of men. / Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras—my subjects—
should dwell in happiness on the earth together with their families. / This illustrious Pūru will be your protector here.
He has been installed by me, O people, as a steadfast king bearing the sceptre.” / Addressed in this manner, all those subjects said to the king:
“It is heard in all the Vedas and Purāṇas, O best of kings, / that dharma was never seen thus by anyone in the world formerly.
We have seen that ten-limbed dharma, beloved of truth, / born in the lunar lineage in the great house of Nahuṣa.”
Equipped with hands, feet, and a face, the propagator of all good conduct, / endowed with knowledge and specialized understanding, and a great storehouse of merit,
a mine of virtues, O great king, truly learned! / And the truthful, of great splendor, perform great dharma.
We have seen that dharma in you, who assume any form at will, / you who fulfill desires, who speak the truth in this manner.
Even with three kinds of action, we are unable to abandon you; / wherever you go, there we go, with utmost happiness and merit alone.
Even in hell, wherever you are, there we are, without doubt. / What use are wives, wealth, and enjoyments, and what use are lives and living
without you, O great king? Therefore there is no purpose here. / Only with you, O king of kings, will we go, not otherwise.
Hearing this speech of the subjects, the lord of the earth, / seized with great joy, spoke these words to the subjects:
“Let all the very meritorious people come along with me.” / The king mounted a chariot with that desire-maiden,
with a chariot white as a swan, resembling the disc of the moon, / fanned with chowries and fans, free from distress,
with that auspicious, white, and very magnificent banner, / shining like the divine king of the gods, Puraṃdara.
Praised by sages, bards, and Cāraṇas, / and praised by his subjects, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa,
and all the subjects then approached the lord of men in vehicles, / on elephants, horses, and various chariots, and set out toward heaven:
brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and other ordinary people, / all of them Vaiṣṇava people, devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu.
Their banners were white, adorned with golden staffs, / all marked with conches and discs, having staffs and carrying pennants.
Amid the throngs of subjects, pennants stirred by the wind shone; / all were wearing divine garlands, adorned with tulasī leaves,
their limbs smeared with divine sandalwood, anointed with divine fragrant perfumes, / made splendid by divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments.
All those people of handsome form approached the king: / hundreds of thousands, hundreds of lakhs and crores of subjects,
thousands of billions—those people set out. / They, all those Vaiṣṇavas who performed meritorious deeds,
all devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu, intent on silent recitation and charity, [set out] together with the king. / Sukarma said: Thus they all set out, filled with great joy.
Having consecrated his son Pūru in his kingdom, O great king, / Yayāti, the lord of the earth, then went to the world of Indra.
By his splendor, merit, dharma, and ascetic practice, / all those people then set out to the supreme world of Viṣṇu.
Then the gods, along with Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas, / together with the king of the gods, came forward to meet him.
Honoring that king of kings himself, O best of kings, / Indra said: “Welcome to you, O great king! Enter my dwelling.
Enjoy here divine pleasures, desires that follow the heart.” / The king said: “O thousand-eyed one, O very wise one, to your two lotus feet
I bow, O god; I am going to the world of Brahmā.” / And being praised by the gods, he went to the world of Brahmā.
The lotus-born [Brahmā] of great splendor, along with the foremost sages, / then offered him hospitality with water for the feet, arghya, and comfortable seats,
and said: “Go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu by your own deed.” / Thus addressed by the Creator, he went to the abode of Śiva.
Śaṃkara, along with Umā, performed the hospitable worship / of that king of kings himself, and said this to the king:
“You are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, O king of kings, and you are very dear to me as well; / therefore, O king Yayāti, dwell in my abode.
Enjoy all pleasures that are hard to obtain for human beings. / There is no difference, O king of kings, between me and Viṣṇu, without doubt.
He who is in the form of Viṣṇu is himself Rudra, without doubt; / and he who is Rudra, O king, is also the eternal Viṣṇu.
There is no difference between the two; therefore indeed I say: / I give my very own abode to a meritorious devotee of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O great king, sinless one, you should certainly stay here.” / Thus addressed even by Śiva, Yayāti, beloved of Hari,
bowing with devotion to the lord of gods, Śaṃkara, with neck bent low: / “All this, O Mahādeva, has now been spoken by you.
There is no difference between you two; one form has become twofold. / I wish to go to the [world] of Viṣṇu; I bow to your feet.”
“May it be so, O great king! Go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.” / Directed thus by Śiva, the lord of the earth set out.
The lord of the earth [went] with those most meritorious Vaiṣṇavas, beloved of Viṣṇu, / who were then dancing before that king.
To the sin-destroying sounds of conches and abundant lion-roars, / the king advanced with sounds [of praise], being honored by noble Cāraṇas.
Sung of in melodious tones by reciters skilled in the treatises, / Gandharvas devoted to singing sang before him.
Praised by sages, accompanied by hosts of gods, / served by apsarases of lovely form, the son of Nahuṣa,
by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas bringing sacred good fortune, / by Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, the king [was praised], and likewise by Maruts, Vasus,
Rudras, classes of Ādityas, and world-protectors, lords of the cardinal directions; / being praised on all sides by the three worlds, O great king,
he saw the world of Viṣṇu, incomparable and free from illness, / filled, O king, with golden aerial chariots, complete with all splendor,
adorned with aerial chariots white as swans, jasmine, and the moon, / with hundred-storied palaces resembling Meru and Mandara,
with spires scraping the sky, made of celestial gold; / with blazing pinnacle-pitchers the excellent city shone.
Just as the sky shines with the glory of light through multitudes of stars, / with flaming blazing rays of light, it looked as if with eyes.
With various jewels, the world of Hari seemed to laugh with its teeth, / calling to those meritorious Vaiṣṇavas, beloved of Viṣṇu,
by means of flags, O king of kings, with tender shoots moving at their tops, / and with those captivating banner-tops swayed by the breeze.
Adorned everywhere with golden poles and with bells, / and then with gateway-towers and turrets having the brilliance of the sun's light,
with lattice-windows and window-networks, with captivating embrasures, / with the brilliance of streets, and with walls fashioned of gold,
with archways, excellent pennants, and various auspicious sounds, / with pitcher-tops having the discs of wheels, of splendor equal to the disc of the sun,
with great pleasures, hundred courtyards, resembling waterless clouds, / covered with parasols and staffs, adorned with pinnacle-pitchers,
adorned with mansions having the form of clouds of the rainy season, / with those shining pinnacle-pitchers, like the sky [adorned] with stars on the earth,
with arrays of staffs and pennants having the luster of arrays of stars, / resembling crystal, with the splendor of conches and the moon.
Crowded with golden palaces made of various metals, / with aerial chariots by the hundreds of millions and thousands of crores,
and endowed with every enjoyment, Hari's city shines. / Those by whom the god who bears the conch, discus, and mace was worshipped,
by his grace dwell in those houses— / mortals [dwelling] in those entirely meritorious, divine abodes filled with enjoyments,
Vaiṣṇavas of virtuous deeds, their blemishes completely washed away. / Adorned with such sacred mansions is the temple-abode of Viṣṇu,
filled with various trees and groves beautified with sandalwood, / adorned everywhere, O king, with [trees bearing] fruits of every desire,
and with step-wells, ponds, and lakes graced by cranes, / crowded with geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, and beautified by white water-lilies,
and it shines with lakes having hundred-petaled blossoms, great lotuses, adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, / and possessing the color of golden lotuses.
Vaikuṇṭha, enriched with all splendour, adorned with celestial gardens, / filled with divine brilliance and graced by Vaiṣṇavas—
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, beheld Vaikuṇṭha, / the peerless place of liberation, filled with multitudes of gods.
He entered that charming city, free from all burning afflictions, / and beheld Nārāyaṇa, free from disease, the destroyer of all distress,
radiant in aerial chariots, adorned with all ornaments, / dressed in yellow garments, Lord of the Universe, marked with the Śrīvatsa, of great splendour,
mounted upon Garuḍa, accompanied by Śrī, higher than the highest, / the refuge of all the gods' realms, the Supreme Lord,
shining as absolute liberation in the form of supreme bliss, / Hari being served by the great people, the very holy Vaiṣṇavas,
surrounded by hosts of gods, attended by groups of gandharvas / and apsarases—Hari, the great soul who takes away sorrow and pain.
Then the king bowed down to Nārāyaṇa together with his wife; / all the mortal Vaiṣṇavas bowed to Madhusūdana.
All the Vaiṣṇavas who had gone along with the king, O high-minded one, / bowed down to his two lotus feet with devotion, O noble-minded one.
To the noble, radiant king who was bowing down, / Hṛṣīkeśa said: "I am pleased with you, O you of good vows!
Choose a boon, O lord of kings, whatever is in your mind; / I grant it to you without doubt, for you are my devotee, O wise one."
The king said: / "If you are pleased, O God of gods, O Madhusūdana, / grant me constant servitude to yourself, O Lord of the Universe."
Viṣṇu said: / "So be it, O fortunate one; you are my devotee, there is no doubt. / You must dwell in my world, O great king, together with her."
Thus addressed, the great king Yayāti, lord of the earth, / by the grace of that god, reached the world of Viṣṇu, embellished with splendour.
This king dwells in that supreme realm of Viṣṇu.

2.84.m: Sukarmā said: / "This entire narrative that destroys sins has been told to you; / it delivers sons, is divine, and grants great merit.
It is visibly seen in the world, as heard in the story of Yayāti: / Pūru attained a great kingdom, while Turu met with misfortune,
as it happened respectively through the father's favor and anger. / Moreover, it is holy, delivers sons, brings fame, and gives wealth and grain.
Both of them were cursed—both Turu and Yadu. / There is nothing equal to mother and father in bestowing desired fruits.
When a father calls his son with an affectionate heart, / and a mother says, 'Son, son!'—listen to the meritorious fruit of that:
As a son, upon being called, goes towards his mother, / if he goes filled with joy, he obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
He who washes their feet, O highly renowned one, / that son enjoys the fruit of all sacred places through the grace of the two [parents].
From massaging their limbs, moreover, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / The son who sustains his elder with food, clothing, and baths,
merit equal to the gift of the earth is indeed produced for that son. / The Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords; just so is a mother, without doubt.
As the ocean is established in the world consisting of great merit, / just so is a father in this world: so know the ancient poets.
Sukarmā said: / He who abandons or shouts at his father and mother, / that son goes to the hell named Raurava, without a doubt.
The householder who does not support his aged mother and father, / that son goes to hell and will surely experience torment.
The wicked, evil-minded son who reviles his elder, / no expiation for him has ever been seen by the ancient poets.
Knowing thus, O brāhmaṇa, day after day I worship / my mother and father constantly, my head bowed with devotion.
Whatever my elders call and tell me to do or not do, / that I perform without hesitation, according to my own capacity, O Pippala.
By that, supreme knowledge granting liberation has arisen in me, / and by the grace of these two, it moves about within worldly existence.
Whatever mortals residing on earth do, / I, though a householder, know that, as well as whatever occurs in heaven.
Even while staying here, I know the movements of the nāgas, O Pippala. / And through the grace of these two, the three worlds have come under my control.
[It has] gone, O best of vidyādharas; you should worship Mādhava." / Viṣṇu said: / Thus urged by him according to his own duty, Pippala,
bowing to that best of the twice-born, though ashamed, went to heaven. / That righteous Sukarmā also attends upon his elder, O king.
All this pertaining to the sacred ford of parents has been recounted by me to you. / What else shall I tell you? Speak, O wise Vena!

2.85.m: Vena said: / "O Blessed Lord, God of gods, by your grace / the sacred ford of the wife and the peerless sacred ford of the father have been described,
as well as the sacred ford of the mother, O Hṛṣīkeśa, which bestows great merit. / Becoming gracious, speak to me now of the sacred ford of the guru."
The Blessed Lord said: / "I shall describe to you, O king, the supreme sacred ford of the guru, / said to remove all sins and grant the highest state to disciples.
It is the supreme merit of disciples, eternal in the nature of dharma, / the ultimate sacred ford, supreme knowledge, yielding visible fruit.
By whose grace, O king of kings, one enjoys fruit right here, / enjoys happiness in the next world, and obtains fame and renown.
By whose grace, O lord of kings—namely that of the noble guru— / the three worlds, moving and unmoving, are directly perceived by disciples.
The conduct of the worlds and right practice, O prince— / the disciple attains discernment and goes indeed to liberation.
Just as the sun is the illuminator of all the worlds, / so the guru is the illuminator, the supreme path of disciples.
And at night the moon shines, O king, O best of monarchs; / by its brilliance it establishes dominion over all that moves and is still.
