A lamp illuminates the gathering in a house, O best of kings; / by its brilliance it dispels all thick, turbid darkness."
The guru illumines the disciple enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, / by means of teachings that shine with illumination for the disciple, O intelligent one.
The sun is the illuminator by day, the moon is the illuminator by night; / a lamp is the illuminator of the house, always dispelling darkness.
By night, by day, and within the home, the guru always [guides] the disciple; / the guru dispels all of his darkness known as ignorance.
Therefore, O king, the guru is the supreme holy place for disciples; / knowing this, a disciple should worship him at all times.
Knowing the guru to consist of merit through three kinds of action— / in this regard an ancient legendary history is heard by Brahmins:
told as destroying all sins, concerning the great-souled Cyavana. / Cyavana, the best of sages, was born in the family of Bhṛgu.
Once a thought arose in him, O best of kings: / 'When shall I become endowed with knowledge on the earth?'
Day and night he reflected, that best of sages desirous of knowledge. / As he thus reflected, a resolve occurred to the great soul:
'I shall depart on a pilgrimage to sacred places, which grants desired fruits, / abandoning house, lands, and the like, then wife, son, and wealth.'
On the occasion of pilgrimage to holy places, he then roamed the earth; / he undertook the pilgrimage following and reversing the course of the Gaṅgā, O king,
and likewise that of the Narmadā and the Sarasvatī, the lord of sages, / of all rivers such as the Godāvarī, and of the ocean;
and under the pretext of pilgrimage to all other holy places and sacred regions, O best of kings, / and to the auspicious liṅgas of the gods, he wandered.
As he wandered among the supreme sacred places, / his body became pure, shining like the splendor of the sun.
Cyavana shone with radiance, his soul purified by this act; / wandering about, he then arrived at the best of sacred regions,
on the southern bank of the Narmadā, named Amarakaṇṭaka. / He saw the great liṅga that grants liberation to all.
Bowing, praising, and worshiping Siddhanātha, the great lord, / and then beholding Jvāleśvara, and also beholding Amareśvara,
Brahmeśa, Kapileśa, and the excellent Mārkaṇḍeśvara, / having thus completed the pilgrimage, he arrived at Oṃkāra.
Resorting to the shade of a banyan tree, cool and dispelling weariness, / the Brahmin Cyavana, delight of Bhṛgu, sat comfortably.
There he heard a sound uttered by a bird, / endowed with divine speech, accompanied by spiritual and practical knowledge.
A parrot dwelt there, who had lived for a long time, / righteous-minded, named Kuñjala, with four sons and a wife.
He had four sons who delighted their father; / I shall tell you their names, O lord of kings:
The eldest was Ujjvala by name, the second Samujjvala, / the third was named Vijvala, and the fourth Kapiñjala.
Such were the four sons of the great-minded Kuñjala, / that virtuous parrot, devoted to their father and mother.
They roamed attentively in mountain bowers and across continents; / agitated for the sake of food, distressed by hunger,
they satisfied the hunger residing in their bellies, O gentle one, with fruits resembling nectar, / and with water sweet as nectar, O best of kings.
The noble sons carefully deposited ripe, juicy fruits / for food, offering the fruits to the [parent] couple,
and for the sake of their mother, those fortunate ones, filled with devotional disposition. / Having procured food, contented, they ate and recited;
engaged in play there, all of them sported and rejoiced. / Knowing evening time had come, they approached the excellent presence of their father,
arriving with food brought with effort for the sake of their parents, / while that Brahmin, the great-souled Cyavana, watched.
All those birds arrived at their father's lovely nest; / they bowed to both their father and mother, O wise one.
Having brought food to the two, they stood before them; / all those excellent sons were greeted and honored by the father,
and by the mother with compassion, O king, with words full of affection, / and with the cool breeze of their wings, both the mother and father then,
those two birds, refreshed them, O king, / greeting their noble sons with blessings;
and the two of them felt great affection [for the food] offered by them, / fully nourishing and resembling nectar, O best of the twice-born.
Drinking the pure water originating from millions of sacred places, / having retired to their dwelling, with happy and contented minds,
they conducted a divine conversation, very auspicious and destroying sin. / Viṣṇu said: Then the son Ujjvala was questioned by his father Kuñjala:
'Where did you go today, my son, and what unprecedented, / auspicious thing did you see or hear there? Tell that to me, my child.'
Hearing the words of his father Kuñjala, that Ujjvala / then replied to his father, bowing his neck in devotion;
he bowed his head and began an enchanting tale. / Ujjvala said: 'O fortunate one, I go to Plakṣadvīpa every day
with great exertion for the sake of food, O wise one. / In Plakṣadvīpa, O great king, there are many regions,
mountains, rivers, gardens, forests, lakes, / villages, and other cities, joyful with prosperous subjects.
Always contented with happiness, those people dwell rejoicing, / endowed with gifts, merit, and recitation of mantras, accompanied by faith.
In Plakṣadvīpa, O great king, there was a righteous-minded king / of ever virtuous mind, Divodāsa; and his daughter was peerless,
endowed with virtues and beauty, well-behaved, charming and auspicious, / famous by the name Divyādevī, incomparable on earth in beauty.
She was observed by her father, endowed with the charm of beauty and youth; / she was in the prime of her youth, charming and auspicious.
Seeing that daughter Divyādevī, Divodāsa then [thought]: / 'To what noble, excellent bridegroom should this maiden be given?'
Having thus become absorbed in thought and looked around, the best among men, / the king of the earth, beholding the king of the realm of Rūpa...
summoning the noble Citrasena, that best of men, / the great-souled one gave the maiden to the wise Citrasena.
When the time of her marriage arrived, O king, / that Citrasena died by the law of time, indeed.
The righteous king Divodāsa reflected; / summoning noble Brahmins, that prince questioned them:
'When the time of her marriage came, Citrasena went to heaven; / tell me what course of action should there be for her?'
The Brahmins said: 'A maiden's marriage according to rule is seen [in scriptures], O king: / if her husband dies, or does not unite with her,
or is afflicted by a severe illness, or renounces and departs, / or becomes an ascetic, O king, as seen in the treatises on dharma.
The marriage of an unmarried girl is performed by the wise; / as long as she has not reached puberty, another husband is prescribed.
A father should perform her marriage according to rule, without doubt; / so it is ordained in the treatises on dharma by the wise, O king.
Let her marriage be performed!' Thus those best of the twice-born said. / The righteous Divodāsa, urged by the words of the twice-born,
The king made an effort for the marriage, O great king. / Divyādevī was given again in marriage, O best of the twice-born,
To the virtuous Rūpasena, to that high-souled king; / But during the wedding, that ruler of the earth, the king, met with death.
Whenever, O fortunate one, a king became Divyādevī's / Husband, at the arrival of the wedding time he always died.
Twenty-one husbands died in succession, O father! / Thereupon the king of renowned prowess became very sorrowful.
Having deliberated, summoned, and consulted with his ministers, / The lord of the earth conceived a grand plan for a bridegroom's choice assembly.
The kings of Plakṣadvīpa were invited by the high-souled one; / Those devoted to dharma were summoned for the purpose of the svayaṃvara.
Enchanted by her beauty and impelled by death, / The foolish kings fought a battle and died on the battlefield.
Thus, O father, the destruction of those high-souled kṣatriyas occurred. / Overwhelmed with immense grief, Divyādevī went into a forest cave.
The young woman, the intelligent Divyādevī, wept piteously. / Thus, O father, I witnessed there at that time this unprecedented thing.
Therefore, O father, tell me in full detail the cause behind her [fate]."

2.86.m: Kuñjala said: / "I shall speak of that deed of Divyādevī, O dear child, / Everything done by her in her previous birth; hear it as I relate it.
There is a meritorious city named Vārāṇasī, which destroys sin. / In it lived a very wise man, Suvīra by name.
Born into the vaiśya caste, he was richly endowed with wealth and grain. / His wife, O very wise one, was well known by the name Citrā.
Abandoning the conduct of her family, she lived in misconduct; / She showed no respect for her husband and acted according to her own whims.
Devoid of dharma and merit, she practiced only sin; / She constantly reviled her husband and was always fond of quarreling.
She always dwelled in others' houses, wandering from house to house; / Always wicked, she was constantly looking for faults in living beings.
Intent on reviling the virtuous, wicked, she always mocked others. / Knowing her to be ill-behaved and very sinful, Vīra censured her.
Abandoning her, the very wise and intelligent man / Married the daughter of another vaiśya, and lived with her.
Virtuous in soul through righteous conduct, his mind was ever on truth and dharma. / Banished by him, the fierce Citrā wandered the earth.
Having found the company of wicked and sinful men, / She, resolute in sin, then acted as a procuress for them.
That evil-doer then brought about the ruin of the households of virtuous people. / Having summoned a chaste woman, she would entice her with sinful words.
With persuasive words she would then destroy her virtue; / That Citrā would deliver the wife of a virtuous man to another.
Thus a hundred households were ruined by Citrā out of sinful intent; / That very wicked woman provoked fights between husbands and sons.
The sinful woman perturbed the minds of women toward other men, / And she caused conflicts that expanded the realm of Yama.
Having ruined a hundred households in this manner, she later met her death, / And was punished with many chastisements by the king of justice, O good son.
The son of the Sun caused her to experience the severe Raurava hells; / In Raurava, Citrā was baked, and various tortures were inflicted upon her.
Whatever sort of deed is done, just such a deed is experienced in return. / A hundred households were ruined by Citrā out of sinful intent.
That ripening of deeds was experienced by her, O best of the twice-born. / Because a hundred households were ruined, she experiences sorrow therefore.
When the time of marriage arrived, fate came to its fruition; / Whenever the time of marriage arrived, her husband met with death.
Just as a hundred households were destroyed, so a hundred suitors died / In the svayaṃvara then, O child, and twenty-one at weddings.
I have told you about Divyādevī as you asked me; / All this former conduct of hers has been related to you."
Ujjvala said: / "You have related the past deed of Divyādevī done formerly, / And the terrible sin called 'household-ruining' committed by her.
By what power of merit was a high lineage attained by her, / The daughter of Divodāsa, the king of Plakṣadvīpa?
Resolve this doubt of mine, O father; tell that to me: / How did one of such sinful conduct become the daughter of a king?"
Kuñjala said: / "I will tell all the virtuous action of Citrā. / Listen, O son Ujjvala, to what was done by Citrā in the past.
Wandering about, a certain wise ascetic arrived, / In rags, lacking clothes, a renunciant bearing a staff,
Wearing a loincloth, using his hands as a bowl, naked, / He approached the doorway of Citrā's house and rested there.
Observing silence, completely shaven, self-conquered, with senses subdued, / Taking no food, one who had mastered eating, beholding the truth of all principles,
Weary from a long journey, his mind distressed by the heat, / Afllicted by exhaustion and overcome by thirst, O good son,
He stood seeking the shade, having approached Citrā's doorway. / That high-souled one, distressed by exhaustion, was seen by Citrā.
Citrā rendered service to that very high-souled one: / Having washed his feet and offered an excellent seat, [she said:]
'Please sit down, O father, in comfort upon this very soft seat, / And to dispel your hunger, please partake of excellent food.
Satisfied to your wish, drink cool water!' / Having spoken thus and acted accordingly, honoring him like a god, O son,
Massaging his limbs, she dispelled his weariness. / Spoken to by her, that high-souled one ate and drank, O best of the twice-born.
Thus the ascetic who beheld the truth of reality was pleased by her. / Satisfied, the completely righteous one remained for a short time.
At his own pleasure, that brahmin, a great yogi, departed the way he had come. / When that fortunate one, that high-souled ascetic, had left,
Citrā met her death, falling under the power of her own karma, / And was punished by Dharmarāja with great, agony-inflicting punishments.
Citrā reached hell, which brings hosts of agonies; / She experienced suffering there, O great king, for a thousand yugas.
At the end of the experiencing, she obtained another birth as a human. / Formerly an ascetic, the foremost among the virtuous, was worshiped by her;
This is the fruit of that deed, that she was born into a family of the virtuous, / In the house of Divodāsa, the great king of the kṣatriyas.
And her name became Divyādevī, O best of men; / For she gave food and pure drink to that high-souled one.
She enjoys the arising of the great fruit of merit of that gift: / She drinks cool water and consumes sweet food.
Enjoying divine pleasures, she lives in her father's palace; / And by the power of that ascetic, she was born as a king's daughter.
And by the power of her sinful karma, from the ruining of households, O ruler of the earth, / Divyādevī suffers widowhood, O good son.
All this conduct of Divyādevī has been related to you. / What else shall I tell you that you ask of me here?"
Ujjvala said: / Tell me, how is she freed from grief, from great suffering? / And what will become of that young woman afflicted by great sorrow?
What sort of happiness [will she have], and what ripening [of karma] will come from that? / You ought to dispel this doubt of mine now, dear father.
Tell me the means, too, by which she may attain liberation. / Alone, the blessed woman weeps aloud in the great forest.
Viṣṇu said: / Having heard his son's weighty question, the very wise Kuñjala / reflected for a moment and answered his son:
Kuñjala said: / Listen, fortunate child; I shall tell you this truth. / Having reached an animal womb born of past actions,
my knowledge was lost through becoming an animal, my son. / But now, through contact with this tree of the pure, great-souled one,
and by the grace of the Revā and the grace of Viṣṇu, / [I know] the means by which she may obtain knowledge and reach the realm of liberation.
I shall explain instruction—the unexcelled path to liberation— / [by which] she will go forth, freed from sin, as gold from fire.
It becomes pure, dear child, having assumed its true nature through contact with fire; / likewise, O very wise one, swiftly through meditation on Hari, that great soul,
the sin of sinners is destroyed through recitation, fire offerings, and vows, / just as an elephant abandons its rutting arrogance always out of fear of a lion.
Through the utterance of Kṛṣṇa's name, that sin indeed departs, / like serpents drained of poison through the splendor of the son of Vinatā [Garuḍa].
Sins such as slaying a brahmin meet destruction—not otherwise; / they depart through the utterance of the name of the Discus-Holder [Viṣṇu].
When she, having become steady and free from desire and anger, / recites the sacred hundred names that destroy masses of evil,
restraining all her sense organs, she should protect [them] through self-knowledge; / entered into meditation on him, unified and concentrated,
she should recite supreme knowledge; then she attains liberation, / when she has her mind fixed on him, absorbed in his state, united in yoga.
Ujjvala said: / Tell me, father, supreme knowledge right now, / and then the sacred vow of meditation and the hundred names right here.
Kuñjala said: / I shall explain supreme knowledge which has not been seen by anyone; / listen, my son, to isolation, absolute and devoid of stain.
Sūta said: / Just as a lamp standing in a windless place, motionless, free of wind, / blazes forth and destroys all darkness, O wise one,
likewise the self, free from defect, becomes supportless; / without desire, pure, dear child, having neither friend nor enemy at any time,
neither sorrow nor joy, neither greed nor envy, / alone, he is freed from dejection and excitement, and from pleasure and pain.
He should withdraw the senses from all sensory objects; / then he becomes isolated, and absolute state comes to be.
By contact with the action of fire, the lamp dries up the oil, / supported by the wick, O best of kings, unattached and free of wind.
Afterward, O wise one, it emits soot from the oil; / that black streak is seen before the lamp, O wise one.
The oil is drawn in by itself; through light it becomes pure. / Likewise, seated in the wick of the body, one should dry up the oil of karma.
Having reduced sense objects to soot, he should reveal directly; / becoming pure, he should produce and illuminate [reality] by himself.
Free from the winds called afflictions, such as anger and the like, / desireless and motionless, he should blaze forth by himself through his own brilliance.
Remaining in his own place, he sees the entire threefold world by his own light. / This nature of absolute knowledge has been described to you by me.
I shall explain the twofold meditation on him, the Discus-wielder; / in the form of absolute knowledge, he is seen with the eye of knowledge.
Great souls united in yoga, devoted to the supreme truth, / sleepless, see him whose austerity reveals all:
he is devoid of hands and feet, yet moves everywhere; / he grasps everything, the moving and the unmoving in the three worlds, my son;
he is devoid of nose and mouth, yet smells and eats, my child; / without ears, he hears everything; he is the witness of all, the Lord of the world;
formless, yet connected to form, subject to the five groups [of elements and senses], / the life-breath of the entire world, worshiped by moving and unmoving beings;
without a tongue, he speaks everything according with the Vedas and scriptures, my son; / without skin, touching is experienced by all [through him].
Ever blissful, detached in self, of uniform nature, without support, / undecaying, unselfish, just, possessing qualities, unselfish, stainless,
unmastered, the self mastering all, bestowing all, knower of all; / he has no creator, and he is the all-pervading Lord composed of all.
Whoever sees such an all-pervading meditation on the great soul, / he goes to the supreme abode, formless, like nectar.
Now I shall tell the second meditation on this great soul: / possessed of form, having concrete shape, [yet] formless and free from illness.
He by whose fragrance the whole incomparable universe is perfumed, / he is therefore called Vāsudeva, my son.
His color is like that of a raining cloud; / resembling the brilliance of the sun, having four arms, the Lord of the gods,
in his right [hand] shines the conch adorned with gold and jewels; / the discus, resembling the solar disc, rests upon a lotus;
his club Kaumodakī, the destroyer of great demons, / shines in the left hand of that great soul, my child;
the great lotus, rich in fragrance, is held in his right hand; / the beloved of Kamalā [Lakṣmī], armed with weapons, is ever radiant.
With a conch-like neck, a round face, and eyes like lotus petals, / the radiant Hṛṣīkeśa, with teeth resembling jewels,
whose hair is curly, whose lower lip has the form of coral, / the Lotus-eyed One shines also with a crown, my son.
Keśava, with a broad form and great splendor, / Janārdana is radiant, marked indeed with the Kaustubha gem.
He shines with ear-ornaments resembling the sun's splendor, / and Hari is ever radiant with the sacred Śrīvatsa mark;
with armlets, bracelets, and necklaces with pearls resembling stars, / shining with his body, victorious, best among victors,
that Govinda also shines with a gold-colored garment; / he is adorned with fingers bearing jeweled rings;
Hari, fully equipped with all weapons and divine ornaments, / mounted upon the son of Vinatā [Garuḍa], the creator of the world, Lord of the universe.
A person who constantly meditates on him thus with an undistracted mind / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
All this meditation on the Lord of the universe has been told to you; / and now I shall tell the vow that removes all sins.

2.87.m: Kuñjala said: / I shall explain the varieties of vows by which Hari has been worshiped: / Jayā, Vijayā, and Jayantī which destroys sin,
Trispṛśā, and another called Vañjulī, likewise another, Tiladagdhā, / Akhaṇḍā, Cārakanyā, and Manorathā, my good son;
and there are many varieties of the eleventh-day vow [ekādaśī], my son, / as well as another, Aśūnyaśayana, and the great vow of Janmāṣṭamī.

By these most meritorious vows, sin goes far away
from living beings, of this there is no doubt; truly, truly do I say.

Kuñjala said:
I shall proclaim his hymn of praise, which destroys masses of sins,
known as the Hundred Names, O good son, which grants the ultimate state to men.

That excellent [hymn] known as the Hundred Names of that god Kṛṣṇa
I will now tell forth; hear it, O best of sons.

I declare the seer and the metre of Viṣṇu's hundred names,
and also the deity, O fortunate one, which purifies all sins.

Brahmā is declared to be the seer of the hundred names of Viṣṇu, / the syllable Oṃ is said to be the deity, and the metre is anuṣṭubh.

The ritual application of this hymn of the hundred names of Viṣṇu / is for the attainment of all desires and for liberation.

Brahmā is the seer; Viṣṇu is the deity; the metre is Anuṣṭubh;
the application is for the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all sins.

I bow to Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, Madhusūdana,
the destroyer of all demons, Nārāyaṇa, the free from affliction,

to Jayanta, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, and then Ananta, Vāmana,
to Viṣṇu, the lord of the universe, the holy one, the support of the universe, worshipped by the gods,

the sinless one, the slayer of sin, Narasiṃha, dear to Śrī,
the lord of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī, the giver of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the source of great prosperity,

Śrīrāma, Mādhava, liberation, the embodiment of forbearance, Janārdana,
the omniscient, the knower of all, the giver of all, the leader of all,

Hari, Murāri, Govinda, Padmanābha, Prajāpati,
bliss, endowed with knowledge, the giver of knowledge, the lord of knowledge,

Acyuta, the strong one, the moon, discus in hand, the higher and the lower,
the support of the cosmic ages, the source of the universe, the form of Brahman, the great lord,

Mukunda, true Vaikuṇṭha, of uniform nature, the lord of the world,
Vāsudeva, the great soul, devoted to sacred learning, fond of brahmins,

fond of cattle, beneficial to cattle, sacrifice, the limb of sacrifice, the nourisher of sacrifice,
the full enjoyer of sacrifice, the one who has mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas,

the knower of the Vedas, the embodiment of the Vedas, the abode of learning, the lord of the gods,
the unmanifest, the supreme swan, conch in hand, the ancient one,

Puruṣa, lotus-eyed, the Boar, the upholder of the earth,
Pradyumna, Kāmapāla, Vyāsa, the serpent, the great lord,

all happiness, great happiness, liberation, the supreme lord,
the form of yoga, great knowledge, the giver of the goal to yogins, the beloved,

Murāri, guardian of the world, lotus in hand, holding a mace,
dwelling in the cave, dwelling in all, the abode of merit, mighty-armed,

lord of Vṛndā, large-bodied, purifying, destroyer of sins,
lord of the cowherdesses, friend of the cowherds, Gopāla, refuge of herds of cows,

supreme self, lord of the beyond, Kapila, human by work—
to him, immovable and eternal, I bow with mind, speech, body, and deeds.

Whoever, performing great merit, praises Kṛṣṇa with a steady mind by these hundred names,
leaving behind the worlds here, purified by merit, goes to the world of Madhusūdana.

He should recite the most meritorious hundred names, which purifies all sins,
with a single-pointed mind, and should meditate on him endowed with contemplation.

A man constantly obtains through merits the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā;
therefore, becoming completely steady and composed in mind, one should recite.

And if a mortal recites at the three junctures of the day, restrained and established in observance,
for him the fruit of a horse sacrifice arises; of this there is no doubt.

Whoever fasts on the eleventh day and recites it during the night-vigil
in the presence of Mādhava—I shall speak of the merit of that mortal:

The man obtains the fruit of a Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
If a man recites it mentally while standing near a tulasī plant,

within a year the man enjoys the fruit of a royal consecration.
Where there is a Śālagrāma stone and where there is a Dvārāvatī stone,

in the presence of both, recitation should be performed by one desiring happiness.
Having enjoyed abundant happiness, that mortal delivers a hundred families,

and one more besides, along with himself.
One who bathes in the month of Kārttika and worships Madhusūdana,

and who, self-controlled, recites the hymn, goes to the supreme state.
One who bathes in Māgha, worships Hari, Madhusūdana, with devotion,

and meditates upon Hṛṣīkeśa, or recites, or listens,
casting aside sins such as drinking liquor, goes to the supreme abode,

O son, and reaches Janārdana without obstacle.
Indeed, which mortal at the time of a śrāddha, in front of the brahmins while they eat,

recites the hymn of the hundred names that destroys sins,
his ancestors attain satisfaction and, fully satisfied, go to the supreme state.

A brahmin becomes learned in the Vedas; a kṣatriya gains the earth;
a vaiśya who recites it constantly enjoys abundance of wealth;

a śūdra enjoys happiness and attains the state of a brahmin;
upon obtaining another birth, dear child, he acquires Vedic knowledge.

This hymn gives happiness and gives liberation; it should be recited without doubt.
By the grace of Keśava, a man becomes successful in everything.
